alt: The Identities theme, which explores the nature of the self and what it means to be human, is linked to five recommended topics: lifestyles, health and well-being, beliefs and values, subcultures, and language and identity. Below, the key question how do language and culture contribute to forming an identity is shown as a lens for any text.
caption: Five recommended topics and one key question to apply to any text.

alt: A balance with two equal pans of 50 percent. Paper 2 listening and reading, on unseen texts, weighs the same as Paper 1 writing and the oral together. A note says fluent speaking on Identities does not automatically transfer to comprehension of unseen texts.
caption: Paper 2 alone weighs as much as writing and the oral together: build comprehension vocabulary too.

after: ## Worked example: applying the key question to an unseen text
alt: Three linked cards: the surface content (traditional dress has changed over time), the specific detail to find (what changed, when and why), and the broader theme question (how the change reflects a shift in how the community's identity is expressed across generations). Below, only extracting facts is contrasted with connecting detail to theme.
caption: The skill tested is linking a specific detail to the broader theme question.

alt: Three cards show the broad text-type categories with examples: personal (blog post, diary entry, letter to a friend), highlighted as often suiting Identities; professional (formal letter, report); and mass media (article, interview). A note says the exam instructions set the text type and register is assessed alongside content.
caption: Personal texts often suit Identities, but the exam sets the type and conventions are marked.

alt: A table pairs three pitfalls with fixes: summarising surface content instead of connecting to the key question; assuming speaking practice guarantees comprehension instead of practising unseen texts; and ignoring register instead of following the text type's conventions.
caption: Apply the theme as a lens, practise unseen texts, and respect text-type conventions.
